reason: The sources provide sufficient information to support a surprising 45-second story about space decompression myths with multiple corroborated claims.
story: Pop culture loves to show astronauts exploding in the vacuum of space. But science tells a completely different story. When exposed to a vacuum, your blood does not boil, you do not instantly freeze, and you certainly do not explode like a balloon. Thanks to the remarkable strength and elasticity of human skin, your body holds its shape. In December 1966, NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc experienced this firsthand when his spacesuit accidentally depressurized in a massive vacuum chamber. LeBlanc remained conscious for about 14 seconds before losing consciousness from lack of oxygen, and he even recalled the saliva on his tongue starting to bubble. A colleague quickly provided oxygen, and LeBlanc recovered almost immediately with no permanent damage. While the vacuum of space is undeniably lethal due to lack of pressure and oxygen, movie myths about instantaneous explosive vaporization are completely false.
angle: Human skin is strong and elastic enough to prevent your body from exploding in the vacuum of space, contrary to persistent Hollywood myths.

claims.claim: Exposure to the vacuum of space does not cause a human body to explode.
In the vacuum of space, human blood does not instantly boil.
A human exposed to a vacuum does not instantly freeze.
In December 1966, NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc was accidentally exposed to a near vacuum when his spacesuit hose detached.
During the vacuum test accident, LeBlanc's suit pressure dropped from 3.8 psi to 0.1 psi in less than 10 seconds.
LeBlanc remained conscious for about 14 seconds before losing consciousness due to hypoxia.
LeBlanc's last conscious memory was feeling the saliva on his tongue start to bubble.
A colleague entered the vacuum chamber within 25 seconds to give LeBlanc oxygen.
LeBlanc recovered almost immediately with just an earache and no permanent physical damage.
Exposure to vacuum for up to 30 seconds is unlikely to cause permanent physical damage.
Animal experiments show rapid and complete recovery is normal for vacuum exposures shorter than 90 seconds.

disputed: Exact timing details of the depressurization rescue vary slightly across narratives, but official NASA records confirm the core timeline of roughly 14 to 25 seconds.
